problem.text: The runtime foundation connects the Python model and generation APIs to native tensor operations, extension compilation, device bookkeeping and reusable storage utilities.

limitations: No extension build, package import, CUDA kernel execution or performance benchmark was performed. The successful computation checks scalar indexing and capacity arithmetic, not GPU execution.

The scalar checks use small Python integers without overflow and do not reproduce cuBLAS accumulation, CUDA half arithmetic, approximate transcendental instructions, stream ordering or memory alignment.

The inspected wrappers do not uniformly validate device, contiguity, dtype and vector-width requirements. Odd-length activation and softcap indexing problems are demonstrated by scalar emulation; whether application call sites admit those shapes remains unverified.
HIP-specific flags and compatibility branches do not establish working ROCm support: the shared primitives also contain NVIDIA-specific PTX.
The sources do not establish why the 256-element growth quantum, kernel thread counts or GELU cubic coefficient were selected, nor whether alternative values perform better.

chapters.title: Runtime initialization, native interfaces and storage utilities

claims.text: The package initializer re-exports Config, Model, Tokenizer, cache classes, synchronous/asynchronous generation classes and samplers. The version is 0.0.1. This is a direct import-based public facade, not a lazy attribute loader; util similarly re-exports misc helpers.

There are two extension-build paths. setup.py normally constructs a PyTorch CUDAExtension when Torch is installed; the presence of EXLLAMA_NOCOMPILE suppresses that step. At runtime, ext.py first imports exllamav3_ext and invokes torch.utils.cpp_extension.load only after ModuleNotFoundError. Both discover .c, .cpp and .cu files recursively. JIT compilation uses host -Ofast on non-Windows systems, versus setup.py's -O3; both use CUDA -O3 and -lineinfo. Windows JIT handling searches for MSVC when cl is absent and adds cuBLAS and virtual-environment library paths. Thus precompilation and deferred compilation are supported alternatives, but their host optimization settings are not identical.

maybe_set_arch_list_env preserves an explicit TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST. Otherwise, on CUDA builds it collects visible-device capabilities, clamps each to the highest SM capability advertised by Torch, deduplicates and sorts the targets, and appends +PTX to the last target. It runs when arch_list is imported and again before JIT loading. The source explicitly assumes the user's NVCC matches Torch's build toolchain; this clamp is a compatibility heuristic, not independent compiler detection.

bindings.cpp exposes ordinary pybind functions for safetensors I/O, normalization, softcapping, Hadamard construction/transforms, trellis quantization and packing, reconstruction, EXL3 GEMM, FP16 GEMM, rotary embeddings, gated activations, sampling and string matching. This is the local interface to the loading, quantizer, quantized-inference, modules and sampling subsystems. The inspected activation, normalization, softcap and hgemm wrappers select the input tensor's device with OptionalCUDAGuard and use Torch's current CUDA stream; their outputs are supplied by the caller rather than allocated by these wrappers.

DeviceContext is lightweight bookkeeping: a global dictionary keys contexts by configuration UUID and device string. Acquisition creates or reuses a context and increments its reference count; release decrements it and removes the entry at zero. The context stores the configuration and device, but does not itself allocate GPU buffers or implement a cache scheduler.

Memory budgeting adjusts Torch's per-process allocator fraction rather than allocating a reservation buffer. After a small 32×32 device computation, set_memory_fraction_reserve uses (free − reserve)/total; set_memory_fraction_use uses min((already_allocated + use)/total, 1). The reserve path does not clamp invalid budgets. unset_memory_fraction restores 1.0, while free_mem combines Python garbage collection with empty_cache. list_gpu_tensors is a diagnostic traversal of globals, thread frames and reachable containers, reporting tensor-object sizes in integer MiB; it is not a storage-deduplicated allocator accounting system.

SeqTensor separates logical sequence length from allocated capacity. Its own PAGE_SIZE is 256, matching the separately declared shared constant numerically. Appending grows storage with torch.cat when end_pos >= capacity, selecting (end_pos // 256 + 1) × 256, then copies into a narrow view. Consequently an exact page boundary still gets another page. clear and truncate retain storage; torch and torch_slice return views, whereas slice and clone construct copied SeqTensors. get_for_device separately caches device copies inside a dictionary and explicitly requires tensors to remain read-only; buffered_arange extends that caching to reusable ranges.

A standard-library simulation of 4,096 single-element appends preserved a positive spare capacity of at most 256 elements, performed 16 growth operations and ended at capacity 4,352. This verifies the capacity arithmetic, not tensor copying. Fixed-size growth bounds unused sequence slots, but unlike geometric growth it repeatedly copies the accumulated allocation as a sequence becomes longer.

hgemm implements row-major C = A @ B through column-major cuBLAS by reversing the operands and calling with dimensions (N, M, K), leading dimensions (N, K, N), alpha = 1 and beta = 0. This represents Cᵀ = BᵀAᵀ without an explicit transpose buffer. It validates half dtype, rank two and compatible dimensions, but does not check contiguity or matching devices.

Scalar address emulation matched ordinary row-major multiplication for all 512 combinations of M, K and N from 1 through 8. This checks the hgemm operand reversal and leading-dimension identity, not cuBLAS numerical accuracy or speed.

The shared elementwise kernels emphasize vectorized caller-owned buffers. silu_mul and gelu_mul process two half elements per thread with 256-thread blocks and fuse activation with multiplication by the second input. SiLU uses half arithmetic; GELU converts to float for 0.5x[1+tanh(c(x+0.044715x³))], with c documented as sqrt(2/π). tanh_opt uses an exponential identity under USE_ROCM or older CUDA architecture/runtime conditions, otherwise tanh.approx.f32. softcap computes scale × tanh(x/scale), using scalar float or paired half loads with float intermediates and 1,024-thread blocks.

The bounded computation gives sqrt(2/π) = 0.7978845608028654, consistent with GELU's literal. It also exposes vector-tail constraints: activation indexing leaves the last element unwritten for tested odd lengths 1, 3 and 513. Emulating half-softcap launch/index arithmetic gives an access beyond length 3, while lengths 1 and 2,049 leave their last element unprocessed. These are indexing results, not observed GPU memory faults.

rms_norm launches one 1,024-thread block per row, loads groups of four elements, accumulates squares in float and reduces first across lanes and then across warps. It computes x × (w + constant_bias) / sqrt(mean(x²) + epsilon), supporting half/float input-output combinations with half weights. Width must be divisible by four. Half inputs are clamped to ±65,504 before normalization; float inputs are not. The wrapper checks weights and shapes, but classifies every non-float input/output as half, so its final invalid-dtype branch does not protect against arbitrary other dtypes.

The clamp value 65,504 is exactly the largest finite binary16 number: (2 − 2⁻¹⁰) × 2¹⁵. A standard-library binary16 decode of bit pattern 0x7bff confirmed that value. This explains the numeric boundary without establishing how the GPU clamp handles every exceptional input.

The low-level utility layer supplies aligned half4/half8 aggregates, 64/128-bit vector transfers, bit reinterpretation/XOR helpers and shape/dtype assertion macros. static_for_pack turns a list of integer constants into compile-time callback instances for specialized kernel dispatch. reduction.cuh supplies 32-lane shuffle reductions and shared-memory aggregation for argmax, half maximum and float sum. Unlike the sum/max helpers, block_reduce_argmax reads all 32 shared warp slots without a num_threads guard, so its use requires all those slots to have been populated.

ptx.cuh exposes m16n8k16 tensor-core operations with either float or half accumulators, shared-memory matrix-fragment loads, 16-byte asynchronous global-to-shared copies, commit/wait groups and GPU-scope barrier operations. These form the local native machinery relevant to quantized inference: data can move into shared memory and then tensor-core fragments without an ordinary scalar matrix representation. Additional helpers provide low/high unsigned multiplication and extraction from a combined 64-bit word. The source warns against its older m8n8k4 helper and records a suspected Blackwell issue with explicitly predicated asynchronous copies; those comments are not measurements reproduced here.

The remaining Python utilities support configuration and diagnostics. read_dict tries ordered alternative keys, including nested '->' paths, checks types and permits integer/float conversions when appropriate; None is treated as missing. disk_lru_cache persists JSON-keyed results through shelve beside the launching script, but implements no eviction despite its name. synchronized uses one shared reentrant lock. Timer measures wall-clock intervals without GPU synchronization; cuda_sync_active synchronizes only devices reporting allocated Torch memory. ProgressBar wraps Rich, becomes inactive for empty text and marks non-transient progress complete on context exit.
